name: Argentina
summary: A South American republic that declared independence from Spain in 1816. In the early 20th century it was one of the richest countries in the world; later it went through coups, debt crises and recovery.

knownFor.label: Tango
knownFor.note: A dance and music born in the port neighbourhoods of Buenos Aires and Montevideo.

knownFor.label: Gauchos
knownFor.note: Horse-riding cattle herders of the pampas, also important as soldiers in the independence wars.

knownFor.label: Asado
knownFor.note: Beef grilled over wood fire, part of national life.

location.value: Southern South America; about 2.78 million km², the eighth-largest country in the world.

terrain.value: The Pampas plains, the Andes in the west (Aconcagua, 6,959 m, the highest point in the Southern and Western Hemispheres) and Patagonia in the south.

climate.value: Temperate in the Pampas; subtropical in the north; cold and windy in Patagonia.

resources.value: Rich farmland: a top beef producer and one of the largest producers of soybeans, maize and sunflower seed.

disasters.value: Floods on the Pampas, droughts, and earthquakes in the Andes (San Juan, 1944).

population.value: About 1.8 million in 1869; about 46 million today.

urbanisation.value: About 60% of people live in the Pampas region, including 15 million in Buenos Aires province.

disease.value: Yellow fever in Buenos Aires (1871) killed about 8% of the city.

migration.value: Mass waves of European immigrants, mainly Italians and Spaniards, second only to the United States.

economicBase.value: Exports of beef, wheat and wool; later industry; today soybeans, cars and energy.

tradeRoutes.value: Railways (many British-built) carried crops to the port of Buenos Aires for Europe.

wealth.value: By 1908 among the seven wealthiest developed countries; repeated crises since.

moneyAndTax.value: High inflation and several defaults; riots forced the president to resign in 2001, and the government defaulted again in 2020.

inequality.value: Land was concentrated in large estates (estancias); workers’ movements grew in the 20th century.

governmentType.value: A federal presidential republic; the armed forces overthrew six governments between 1930 and 1976.

keyRulers.value: José de San Martín (independence); Domingo Sarmiento; Juan and Eva Perón; Raúl Alfonsín (1983); Néstor Kirchner (2003).

succession.value: Elections, often interrupted by coups; democracy since Raúl Alfonsín’s election in 1983.

institutions.value: The 1853 constitution, Congress, provinces, the Supreme Court.

stability.value: The military junta of 1976–83 persecuted and murdered thousands of critics and activists in the “Dirty War”, a period of state terrorism.

eliteConflict.value: Long conflict between Buenos Aires and the provinces; later between Peronists and anti-Peronists.

armyAndTech.value: Armies of independence (San Martín crossed the Andes in 1817).

majorWars.value: The War of Independence (1810–25) and the Falklands War with Britain (1982).

territoryChange.value: The “Conquest of the Desert” (1878–84) took Patagonia from Indigenous peoples.

alliancesRivals.value: A founding member of Mercosur; the only South American country to send warships to the 1991 Gulf War.

inventions.value: Fingerprint classification for police (Vucetich, 1891), the ballpoint pen (developed by Bíró in Buenos Aires, 1943), the bus (colectivo).

scienceEducation.value: Several Nobel Prizes in the sciences, beginning with Bernardo Houssay.

openness.value: Very open to immigration and trade before 1930; more protectionist after.

communicationTransport.value: British-built railways across the Pampas (by 1914 about 33,000 km); the port of Buenos Aires.

religion.value: Mainly Catholic; Jorge Mario Bergoglio, Archbishop of Buenos Aires, was elected Pope Francis in 2013.

languageWriting.value: Spanish, mostly the Rioplatense dialect, with strong regional variation.

artsArchitecture.value: Tango (its golden age was the 1930s to mid-1950s) and Jorge Luis Borges, Argentina’s most acclaimed writer.

socialStructure.value: A large middle class for Latin America, but rising poverty during crises.

sharedIdentity.value: A strong sense of national identity built on immigration, the gaucho and the Malvinas/Falklands claim.

dailyLife.value: City apartments and conventillos for immigrants; estancias on the Pampas; beef, bread, mate tea.

neighbours.value: Chile, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and Uruguay.

ideasReligions.value: Liberal ideas from Europe; later Peronism, a movement mixing nationalism and workers’ rights.

colonisation.value: Claims the Falkland Islands (Malvinas), held by Britain since 1833.

riseSignals.value: The War of Independence (1810–25) and the Declaration of Independence on 9 July 1816.

peakPeriod.value: The “golden age” of farm exports, about 1880–1914.

declineSignals.value: The Great Depression led to the first coup (1930) and the “Infamous Decade” (1930–43).

sources.value: Wikipedia: Argentina; Wikipedia: History of Argentina.

overallCertainty.value: Well documented; numbers of victims of the dictatorship are disputed.
